catalog_quote: 1. In words of two syllables the accent is usually on the first syllable, as 'kune: first; 'numa: house. (a) Sometimes, however, it is on the second syllable, as po'ra, rotten, vi'ro, flesh, a'pae, women. 2. In words of three syllables the accent is usually on the second syllable, as ku'nena, first, ri'pana, knows. (a) Occasionally it is on the last syllable, as kiro'ro, kingfisher. (b) Sometimes the first syllable is accented, as 'kamura, big; 'rigolo, year. 3. Words of four syllables are usually accented on the first and third, as 'kori'kori, narrow; 'rapa'luga, tomorrow. (a) Sometimes they are stressed on the second and fourth, as ve'wave'wa, bright; a'paea'pae, women. (b) Sometimes on the second only, as gi'vavina, aunt; ma'parara, all. 4. Polysyllabic words are usually stressed on the first and alternate syllables, as 'aunili'malima, people; 'rapa'luga'lugana, morning. (a) Sometimes the stress is on the second and fifth, as ka'kewaka'kewa. (b) Sometimes it is on the first and fourth, as 'kalova'kalova, red. Notes. Re 1(a). The final syllable in such cases is usually a contraction or a diphthong. In Keapara these words appear as po'raha, vi'roho. Re 3(a). Words that are duplicates keep the accent of the simple form. ... Words of different meaning but identical spelling are often differentiated by their stresses. 'ara (our) friend; a'ra garden; 'kopa distended; ko'pa to skin; 'koma hard, black stone; ko'ma sore, wound. 'rina seasand; ri'na riches

new_statements.rule_in_words: Default: main stress on the penultimate syllable (2-syll initial, 3-syll second, 4-syll first+third, longer words first and alternate syllables, i.e. alternating rhythm from the left landing on the penult), but the position is not fully predictable: Short lists lexical exceptions with final stress (po'ra, vi'ro, a'pae, kiro'ro), antepenultimate stress ('kamura, 'rigolo, gi'vavina, ma'parara), and stress-only minimal pairs ('ara/a'ra, 'kopa/ko'pa, 'koma/ko'ma, 'rina/ri'na). Dutton 1970:889 restates this as 'stress is phonemic'. A coder preferring the dominant pattern would enter fixed: penultimate syllable with lexical exceptions.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Four-syllable words carry stress on first and third syllables; polysyllables on first and alternate syllables (variants: second and fourth; second and fifth; first and fourth); Short does not say which of the two stresses is primary. Reduplicated words keep the stress of the simple form.
new_statements.exceptions: Final-stressed disyllables (po'ra, vi'ro, a'pae) 'usually a contraction or a diphthong' — Keapara cognates keep the lost syllable (po'raha, vi'roho); trisyllables occasionally final (kiro'ro 'kingfisher') or initial ('kamura, 'rigolo); four-syllable words sometimes on second only (gi'vavina, ma'parara); reduplications keep base stress; homographs distinguished by stress alone ('ara/a'ra, 'kopa/ko'pa, 'koma/ko'ma, 'rina/ri'na). Dutton 1970:889 adds that stress is 'related to syllable length (in that all long syllables are stressed)', which is his inference, not stated on Short's stress page.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement on citation forms (isolated words with glosses); intonation treated separately (p. 4: 'The intonation of the Hula tongue is descending'). Impressionistic 1930s description by a resident missionary-teacher; no instrumental data.
new_statements.identity_note: Short 1938 describes the Hula dialect proper (Hula village, Hood Bay; Glottolog hula1239, ISO hul), with separate notes on neighbouring Keapara dialects (keap1239) on thesis pp. 114-118; her Keapara comparisons (po'raha, vi'roho) refer to keap1239, not Hula. Dutton 1970 cites the thesis as 'Short (1939)'; the Adelaide record and title page give M.A. 1938. Not to be confused with hula1244 (Jewish Neo-Aramaic of Sanandaj, 'Hulaula') already in the catalog.
